Each traversed edge, in the accent color, is labeled with its step numbers from 0; A to B is taken twice, at steps 0 and 3. The card lists the 6 edges in order." width="100%"} Like `random_walk()`, but records the sequence of edges crossed rather than nodes visited. At each step the walker picks uniformly at random among the edges it may follow from its current node (edge weights are ignored), so parallel edges are distinguished and each counts separately. The result can be returned as a list of edge tuples, or the traversal order can be stored as an edge attribute for visualization. The edge view is the natural one for edge-centric analyses, such as: - estimating how heavily each edge is used by a random process (traffic, diffusion) - highlighting the route a walker took when drawing the graph - comparing several walks edge by edge Time complexity: `O(steps * m)`, since each step scans the edge list for the edges incident to the current node. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [source]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The node where the walk begins, given as an integer node ID or a string label. A string is always a label, even one made only of digits (such as `"3"`). [steps]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Number of edges to traverse. A complete walk returns exactly `steps` edges; with `steps=0` the result is empty. [mode]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [["out"]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Which edges the walker may follow on a directed graph: `"out"` (default) follows outgoing edges, `"in"` follows incoming edges backwards, and `"all"` follows edges in either direction. For undirected graphs every mode follows any incident edge. [stuck]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [["return"]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default} : What to do when the walker reaches a node with no edge it can follow under `mode=`. With `"return"` (default), the walk stops and the edges crossed so far are used. With `"error"`, a `RuntimeError` is raised instead. [seed]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Integer seed for the random number generator. The same seed on the same graph always produces the same walk. If `None` (default), the walk is seeded from system entropy and differs from call to call. [attr_name]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of the edge attribute that receives each edge's position in the walk. If `None` (default), the attribute is called `random_edge_walk_order`. Positions are 0-indexed (the first edge crossed gets `0`). An edge crossed several times keeps the position of its *last* crossing; edges never crossed get no value. Ignored when `return_list=True`. [return_list]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `False` (default), store the traversal order as an edge attribute (see `attr_name=`) and return the graph for method chaining. If `True`, leave edge attributes untouched and return the list of edge tuples. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[tuple[int, int, int]] | Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `return_list=True`: List of (edge_id, source_id, target_id) tuples. For undirected graphs each pair is oriented in the direction walked; for directed graphs it is the edge's own source and target. If `return_list=False`: Self for method chaining, with edge traversal order stored as edge attributes. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `source=` does not exist, `mode=` is not one of `"out"`, `"in"`, `"all"`, or the walk gets stuck and `stuck=` is not `"return"` or `"error"`. [RuntimeError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If walk gets stuck and `stuck="error"`. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Where `random_walk()` tracks the sequence of nodes visited, this variant records the sequence of edges *traversed*, which is the natural view for edge-centric analyses. Counting how many times each edge appears across a long walk gives a Monte Carlo estimate of the stationary edge-transition probability, which turns into an edge-importance ranking, a graph-sketching primitive, or a sanity check against analytic transition matrices. Because it returns `self` when `return_list=False` and stores per-walk attributes under a customizable name, several walks can be chained side by side under different attribute labels and later compared without recomputation. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Walking a triangle for 5 steps returns 5 traversed edges, each as an `(edge_id, source_id, target_id)` tuple. Because the graph is undirected, each tuple is oriented in the direction the walker actually moved: ::: {#c3f0eb3c .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A")]) ) graph.random_edge_walk("A", steps=5, seed=23, return_list=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [(1, 1, 2), (2, 2, 3), (2, 3, 2), (1, 2, 1), (3, 1, 3)] ``` ::: ::: Rather than returning the list, the traversal order can be stored on each edge as an attribute. After 100 steps on a 3-edge triangle every edge has been crossed, and each records the position of its most recent crossing: ::: {#ef33c5ce .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.random_edge_walk("A", steps=100, seed=23) graph.get_edge_attrs_by_id("random_edge_walk_order") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` {1: 95, 2: 99, 3: 98} ``` ::: ::: Because it returns the graph when `return_list=False`, multiple walks can be chained together under different attribute names for comparison. Here both 50-step walks on a 6-cycle end up crossing all six edges: ::: {#c4e3e537 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_cycle_graph(6) .random_edge_walk(1, steps=50, seed=23, attr_name="walk1") .random_edge_walk(1, steps=50, seed=123, attr_name="walk2") ) walk1_orders = graph.get_edge_attrs_by_id("walk1") walk2_orders = graph.get_edge_attrs_by_id("walk2") # Edges visited by both walks common_edges = set(walk1_orders.keys()) & set(walk2_orders.keys()) len(common_edges) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` 6 ``` ::: ::: Counting crossings over a long walk estimates how heavily each edge is used. On a symmetric triangle, the three edges are crossed roughly equally often: ::: {#abe6495d .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} from collections import Counter graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A")]) ) edges = graph.random_edge_walk(source="A", steps=1000, seed=23, return_list=True) Counter(edge_id for edge_id, _, _ in edges) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` Counter({3: 344, 1: 334, 2: 322}) ``` ::: :::
